title: Anointing the sick
hook: oil and prayer for the sick (James 5:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: hands laid on with prayer, and a church sending its own teachers away. Your line was hands laid on. Who did you thank, and what did you thank them for? Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

A small metal container, about the size of a lipstick, with a screw-top lid. Inside, a pad of cotton soaked in olive oil. A priest carries it in a jacket pocket down a hospital corridor, past the vending machines, into a room where a man lies with a drip in his arm. Across the city, in a living room, a bottle of plain olive oil from the grocery store sits on a coffee table. A few friends from church gather around a woman in an armchair. One of them puts a dab of oil on her forehead with a thumb, and they all begin to pray. Different rooms, the same two things. Today's word is unction.

Unction means an anointing with oil. And for the sick, the instructions come straight from the letter of James, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him." Look at the shape of it. The sick person calls. The church comes. Oil and prayer go together. First, the oil was ordinary. In Mark, the disciples go out and anoint "with oil many that were sick, and healed them." In the parable, the Good Samaritan bandages a stranger's wounds, "pouring in oil and wine." Oil was what you reached for when someone was hurt. James takes that kitchen-shelf remedy and puts it inside a prayer. Second, the Catholic rite. Catholics call it the anointing of the sick, and count it a sacrament. It was once called extreme unction and kept mostly for the dying. Today the Catholic Church offers it to anyone facing serious illness, surgery, or the frailty of age. Third, the Orthodox. They call it Holy Unction, and in some Orthodox parishes, people who aren't bedridden at all come forward to be anointed during Holy Week. Some Protestant churches anoint with oil when elders pray for the sick, just as James describes. Others lay hands on the sick and pray without oil. Fourth, what James promises. The Lord shall raise him up. Some Christians read that as bodily healing. Others hear strength, forgiveness, and company in suffering. People are anointed, and some recover and some don't. The rite says they're not left alone.

Here's the practice: pray for a sick person. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is ill right now: in a hospital, at home, or sick in a way nobody can see. Picture where they are at this moment, the bed, the chair, the light in the room. Sit the way you would in a chair pulled up beside them. If you pray, you can ask God to raise them up, in whatever way that means for them today. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind for a minute, the way the elders in James came when they were called. The bell holds the time.
Unction. An anointing with oil. For the sick, it's oil and prayer together, brought by the church when someone calls, as the letter of James describes.

Your line: oil and prayer. Today, do one ordinary, physical thing for someone who's unwell: soup, a ride, a visit, a message that says you're thinking of them. Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the anointing of the sick as a sacrament for those seriously ill or frail with age; the Orthodox celebrate Holy Unction, in some parishes for all the faithful during Holy Week; some Protestant churches anoint with oil when elders pray for the sick, and others lay on hands and pray.

notes: Mark 6:13 quote begins mid-verse ('anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them'); the spoken line keeps 'anoint' outside the quotation marks. Confirm.

Catholic history: 'once called extreme unction and kept mostly for the dying'; now offered for serious illness, before surgery, and to the frail elderly (CCC 1514–1515). Stated without dates. Confirm.
Orthodox: Holy Unction (Euchelaion) celebrated for all the faithful on Holy Wednesday in some parishes; confirm 'some parishes'.
Original note: εὐχέλαιον combines εὐχή (prayer) and ἔλαιον (oil). This is a compound name, flagged here under the etymology rule; confirm spelling and the note.
'Some Christians read that as bodily healing. Others hear strength, forgiveness, and company in suffering' — attributed, not ranked. Confirm fair.
